trial_name: PAC-Man — Pulmonary Artery Catheter vs No PAC in ICU (2005)
citation: Harvey S, Harrison DA, Singer M, Ashcroft J, Jones CM, Elbourne D, et al; PAC-Man study collaboration. Assessment of the clinical effectiveness of pulmonary artery catheters in management of patients in intensive care (PAC-Man): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2005;366(9484):472-477
one_liner: In adult ICU patients for whom clinicians considered PAC use relevant, a PAC-guided management strategy did not reduce hospital mortality compared with no PAC (68% vs 66%; adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94–1.27).

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with severe illness (multiorgan dysfunction in 65–66%) where treating clinicians intended to use a PAC and had equipoise
pico.intervention: Management with a pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) inserted as soon as possible, with subsequent clinical decisions at clinician discretion
pico.comparison: Management without a PAC (usual care); rescue PAC permitted if equipoise lost (5% of controls); alternative cardiac output monitoring allowed in most ICUs (stratum B)
pico.outcome: Ultimate hospital mortality (death before discharge from acute hospital)

background.existing_knowledge: PACs were widely used for invasive hemodynamic monitoring in ICU, but evidence linking PAC-derived variables to improved patient-centred outcomes was lacking. Observational studies suggested potential harm.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether PAC-guided management improves hospital mortality in routine ICU practice.
background.hypothesis: PAC-guided management would reduce hospital mortality compared with no PAC.

methods.design: Pragmatic, multicentre, open-label RCT in 65 UK adult ICUs; allocation minimised by ICU, age, clinical syndrome, surgical status, and pre-specified ICU stratum (A: no alternative monitoring; B: alternative permitted).
methods.setting: 65 UK adult ICUs; enrolment October 2001 to March 2004.

inclusion: Treating clinician intended to manage with a PAC and had sufficient equipoise to allow randomisation
exclusion: PAC already in situ on ICU admission

methods.intervention: Management with a PAC inserted as soon as possible after randomisation (median time 1.7 h). Subsequent management (fluids, vasoactive drugs, ventilation, renal support) at clinician discretion. PAC remained in place as long as deemed necessary (median first catheter duration 2 days; total indwelling days 3).
methods.comparison: Management without a PAC (usual care). Rescue PAC insertion permitted if clinicians lost equipoise (occurred in 24/522 controls). In stratum B ICUs, alternative cardiac output monitoring devices were permitted in the control arm.
methods.sample_size_power: Initially planned 5673 to detect 5% absolute mortality difference; revised to 1281 to detect 10% absolute difference with 90% power at 5% significance, allowing for non-compliance and 5% loss to follow-up. 1041 randomised, 1014 analysed.
methods.primary_outcome: Ultimate hospital mortality (death before discharge from acute hospital).
methods.follow_up: Until final discharge from acute hospital; in-hospital survival analysed to 90 days.

headline_bullets: No significant difference in ultimate hospital mortality: 68% PAC vs 66% control (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94–1.27, P=0.25).
No differences in ICU mortality, 28-day mortality, length of stay, or organ-support days.
PAC insertion triggered management changes in 80% of cases within 2 hours, but did not translate into outcome benefit.
Direct insertion complications occurred in 10% of PAC placements (none fatal).

outcomes_table.note: Unadjusted HR 1.07 (0.92–1.24), P=0.40; Fisher’s exact P=0.39. One control patient censored (still in hospital at 3 months).
Composite organ-days based on augmented care period dataset.
Haematoma 17 (4%), arterial puncture 16 (3%), arrhythmias requiring treatment 16 (3%), pneumothorax 2, haemothorax 1, lost guidewire retrieval 2; none fatal.

safety: Direct PAC insertion complications occurred in 10% (46/486) of PAC placements: haematoma 4%, arterial puncture 3%, arrhythmias requiring treatment within 1 h 3% (including 1 cardiac arrest), pneumothorax 0.4%, haemothorax 0.2%, lost guidewire retrieval 0.4%; none fatal.

domains.notes: Central 24-hour telephone randomisation with minimisation by ICU, age, clinical syndrome, surgical status, and pre-specified stratum; allocation concealed until assignment.
Unblinded (open-label); primary outcome (mortality) objective, but co-interventions and resource use susceptible to performance bias.
27/1041 excluded post-randomisation (withdrawal/consent), balanced between groups; primary analysis ITT.
Crossover: 5% of controls received PAC (loss of equipoise); 7% of intervention arm did not receive PAC (insertion failure, clinical change, safety).
Groups well matched: mean age 64.7 vs 65.3, APACHE II 22.1 vs 22.7, SOFA 8.6 vs 8.6, median time to randomisation 16.2 vs 15.3 h.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: randomisation and objective mortality endpoint support causal inference for the pragmatic PAC strategy question, but unblinded care, crossovers, and limited power for modest effects constrain interpretability.

domains.notes: Adults in UK ICUs with severe acute illness and high mortality (66–68%); multiorgan dysfunction in 65–66% at enrolment.

Pragmatic delivery reflects real-world clinician decision-making; most patients in stratum B where alternative cardiac output monitoring was permitted (79% in both arms). Excludes elective perioperative optimisation. Findings less applicable to protocolised PAC-driven algorithms or modern echocardiography-dominant practice.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate: results generalise to adult ICUs considering PACs for severe shock/multiorgan failure in settings similar to early-2000s UK practice, but are less informative for specific phenotypes, algorithmic haemodynamic optimisation, or contemporary less-invasive monitoring workflows.

strengths: Large, multicentre pragmatic RCT across 65 ICUs with broad case-mix, enhancing relevance to routine practice.
Central randomisation with minimisation and pre-specified subgroup framework (including ICU policy strata).
Objective primary endpoint (ultimate hospital mortality) with near-complete follow-up (one censored control patient).
Detailed reporting of adherence, early management changes attributable to PAC-derived data, and insertion complications.
limitations: Unblinded design; co-interventions at clinician discretion could dilute any benefit of PAC information.
Permitted rescue crossover (5% of controls received PAC) and some non-delivery in the intervention arm (7% without PAC).
Revised sample size target (1281) not achieved (1041 randomised), limiting exclusion of smaller but clinically meaningful effects.
Trial did not evaluate a standardised treatment algorithm tied to PAC variables, nor quantify competency/interpretation quality.
Control-arm use of alternative cardiac output monitoring was permitted in most participants (stratum B), narrowing inference to the incremental value of PAC over other monitoring strategies.

critical_appraisal.summary: PAC-Man is a well-conducted pragmatic RCT demonstrating no mortality benefit from routine PAC-guided management in a broad ICU population, but unblinded care, crossovers, and lack of protocolised response limit conclusions about efficacy in specific subgroups.
strengths: Large sample size, multicentre, objective primary outcome, detailed process measures.
weaknesses: Unblinded, crossovers, underpowered for modest effects, no treatment algorithm.

sections.authors_conclusion: In adult ICU patients, management with a PAC did not improve hospital mortality compared with management without a PAC.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine PAC use in ICU patients with severe illness does not improve survival and carries procedural risk; selective use may be considered when less invasive monitoring is insufficient and results will change management.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with shock/multiorgan failure where clinicians consider PAC use, in settings similar to early-2000s UK practice.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That PAC-derived physiological data are never useful; benefit may require protocolised treatment algorithms or specific phenotypes.
implementation_caveats: Insertion complications occur in 10% of placements.
Benefit may depend on clinician interpretation and timely therapeutic response.
Alternative monitoring technologies may provide similar information with less risk.

controversies.topic: What question did PAC-Man truly answer?
controversies.notes: The trial compared PAC against a control that often included alternative monitoring, making it an incremental effectiveness trial rather than PAC vs nothing. The no-alternative stratum A was smaller and potentially underpowered.
Lack of benefit may reflect variable interpretation of PAC data and absence of a standardised treatment response, not that PAC-derived physiology is never useful.
Other ICU/acute respiratory failure trials similarly failed to demonstrate improved outcomes from early PAC-guided management, aligning with PAC-Man’s conclusion.
A JAMA meta-analysis and a Cochrane review concluded that PAC use did not reduce mortality in adult ICU populations and did not reliably improve key secondary outcomes.
Observational data show major declines in PAC use across the 1990s–2000s, accelerated by key publications and trials.

Major consensus guidance now frames PACs as a selective tool for complex shock when echocardiography/less invasive monitoring is insufficient and results will change management, rather than routine ICU monitoring.

context_related_trials.relation: Also found no mortality benefit from PAC-guided management in patients with severe heart failure.
Also found no mortality benefit from PAC-guided management in patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

unresolved_questions: Whether protocolised PAC-guided therapy in specific subgroups (e.g., right ventricular failure, pulmonary hypertension) improves outcomes.
Whether modern echocardiography and less invasive monitoring have made PACs obsolete or if there remains a niche for complex shock.

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: 68% vs 66% mortality (adjusted HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.94–1.27)
Management changes within 2h of PAC insertion: 80%
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Routine PAC use in ICU does not improve survival and causes complications; reserve for selected cases where less invasive monitoring is insufficient and results will change management.
